title: Antihistamines and Alcohol: Which Allergy Meds Are Safe?
excerpt: Can you drink on allergy medicine? How drowsy and non-drowsy antihistamines interact with alcohol, which ones are riskiest, hidden ingredients to check, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on allergy medicine? Which antihistamines are risky with alcohol (Benadryl, Zyrtec, Claritin, Allegra), hidden ingredients, warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** it depends on which antihistamine you take. The older, drowsy kind (Benadryl, Unisom, Chlor-Trimeton, hydroxyzine, promethazine, and the sleep ingredient in NyQuil and most "PM" products) should not be mixed with alcohol, because both slow down your brain and the effects add up. The newer, non-drowsy kind (Allegra, Claritin, and to a lesser degree Zyrtec and Xyzal) cause much less sedation, so a drink or two is generally lower risk for a healthy adult, but they're not risk-free and the labels still deserve a read. This guide explains the mechanism, ranks the common allergy medicines, covers the hidden ingredients that cause most of the trouble, and lists the signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on a drowsy antihistamine. Never use Benadryl or a "PM" pill as a sleep aid after a night out. If you need allergy relief and plan to have a drink, a non-drowsy option like fexofenadine (Allegra) or loratadine (Claritin) is the better pick, and you should find out how it affects you on a sober day first. Check every label for acetaminophen, ibuprofen, decongestants, or alcohol hiding in combination products. Don't drive until you know how the combination affects you.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining antihistamines and alcohol if** you are over 65, are pregnant or breastfeeding, take sleep aids, anxiety medicine, opioids, muscle relaxers, antidepressants, or seizure medicine, have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, heart rhythm problems, sleep apnea, or liver or kidney disease. **Call 911** if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or is very confused. For a possible overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## Why Antihistamines and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Histamine is a chemical messenger your body uses for a lot of jobs. In allergies, it's the thing that makes your nose run, your eyes itch, and your skin break out in hives. Antihistamines block the main histamine receptor involved in those symptoms, called the **H1 receptor**.

The catch is that histamine also works inside your brain, where it helps keep you awake and alert. Any antihistamine that gets into the brain and blocks H1 receptors there will make you drowsy. That's the whole story behind why some allergy pills knock you out and others don't.

Alcohol is a **central nervous system depressant**, meaning it slows down activity in the brain. It does this mostly by boosting GABA, the brain's main "calm down" signal, and dampening glutamate, the main "go" signal. When you add a sedating antihistamine on top, you get two different routes to the same place: slower reactions, worse coordination, poorer judgment, and deeper sleepiness. Doctors call this an **additive** (sometimes more than additive) effect. Neither drug changes how the other is broken down in any major way. The problem is simply that their effects pile up in the brain.

### The second problem: anticholinergic effects

The older antihistamines also block a different chemical messenger called acetylcholine. That's called an **anticholinergic** effect, and it explains their familiar side effects: dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, trouble peeing, a faster heart rate, and, at higher doses or in older adults, confusion and memory problems.

Alcohol already causes dehydration, a racing heart, and fuzzy thinking. Stack an anticholinergic drug on top and those effects can get stronger. This is why the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a widely used list of medicines that older adults should generally avoid, includes the first-generation antihistamines. Add alcohol and the risk of falls and confusion in older adults goes up further.

### First-generation vs second-generation: the key difference

Antihistamines are usually sorted into two groups:

- **First-generation (older, drowsy) antihistamines** easily cross the blood-brain barrier, the filter that keeps many substances out of the brain. They cause real sedation and have strong anticholinergic effects. Several of them are sold as sleep aids precisely because they make you sleepy.
- **Second-generation (newer, "non-drowsy") antihistamines** were designed to stay mostly outside the brain. They cause far less drowsiness and have little anticholinergic effect. They're also longer-acting, so most are taken once a day.

That difference is what decides how risky a drink is.

## Antihistamines and Alcohol: A Ranked Guide to Common Allergy Medicines

Here's how the common products compare. "Risk with alcohol" here is about sedation and impairment in a healthy adult at label doses. It is a general guide, not personal advice.

| Antihistamine (common brand) | Generation | Drowsiness on its own | Risk with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diphenhydramine (Benadryl, ZzzQuil, Tylenol PM, Advil PM) | First | High | High. Avoid drinking. |
| Doxylamine (Unisom SleepTabs, NyQuil) | First | High | High. Avoid drinking. |
| Hydroxyzine (Atarax, Vistaril; prescription) | First | High | High. Avoid drinking. |
| Promethazine (Phenergan; prescription) | First | High | High. Avoid drinking. |
| Chlorpheniramine (Chlor-Trimeton, many cold medicines) | First | Moderate | Moderate to high. Avoid drinking. |
| Dimenhydrinate and meclizine (Dramamine, Bonine) | First | Moderate to high | Moderate to high. Avoid drinking. |
| Cetirizine (Zyrtec) | Second | Low to moderate | Moderate. Label says avoid alcohol. |
| Levocetirizine (Xyzal) | Second | Low to moderate | Moderate. Label says avoid alcohol. |
| Loratadine (Claritin) | Second | Low | Lower. Use caution. |
| Desloratadine (Clarinex; prescription) | Second | Low | Lower. Use caution. |
| Fexofenadine (Allegra) | Second | Very low | Lowest of the group. Use caution. |

A few things stand out.

**The drowsy ones are the real hazard.** Benadryl, doxylamine, hydroxyzine, and promethazine can cause heavy sedation on their own. With alcohol, that can turn into dangerous impairment, very deep sleep, and, at higher doses or with other sedatives, slowed breathing. We cover the most common of these in more detail in our guides to [Benadryl and alcohol](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover), [hydroxyzine and alcohol](/never-hungover/hydroxyzine-and-alcohol), and [Dramamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol).

**Zyrtec is in the middle.** Cetirizine is a second-generation drug, but it reaches the brain more than loratadine or fexofenadine and makes a noticeable minority of people drowsy. The US Zyrtec label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks and warns that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness. Levocetirizine (Xyzal) is a close relative and carries similar warnings. See our full guide to [Zyrtec and alcohol](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol) for timing and dosing.

**Allegra and Claritin are the least sedating.** Fexofenadine in particular barely enters the brain at normal doses. That doesn't mean "anything goes." People react differently, alcohol impairs you on its own, and your allergy symptoms can get worse when you drink (more on that below). But if you have hay fever and plan to have a glass of wine at dinner, these are the lower-risk choices. One small tip for Allegra: its label says to take it with water, because fruit juices such as grapefruit, orange, and apple juice can reduce how much of the drug your body absorbs. That matters if your drink of choice comes with a juice mixer.

## The Driving Problem: Why Drowsy Antihistamines Deserve Respect

People tend to treat over-the-counter allergy pills as harmless. The research on driving says otherwise.

A well-known driving-simulator study published in the *Annals of Internal Medicine* in 2000 (Weiler and colleagues, run on the University of Iowa driving simulator) compared people after taking diphenhydramine, fexofenadine, alcohol, or a placebo. Driving performance after diphenhydramine was worse than after alcohol at a blood alcohol level around 0.1%. Fexofenadine performed similarly to placebo. Just as striking, people who'd taken diphenhydramine often didn't *feel* very drowsy, even though their driving was impaired. That gap between how impaired you are and how impaired you feel is exactly what alcohol makes worse.

So the practical rule is simple. **Don't drive after taking a first-generation antihistamine, and absolutely don't drive after combining one with alcohol.** With the newer antihistamines, don't drive after drinking at all if you can avoid it, and especially not until you know how the medicine affects you.

## The Hidden-Ingredient Problem: Where Most of the Risk Actually Lives

The single most useful thing you can do is read the Drug Facts box on anything you take. A lot of products contain an antihistamine you didn't know about, and a lot of antihistamine products contain other drugs that have their own alcohol problems.

### Sleep aids and "PM" products

Most over-the-counter sleep aids are just a first-generation antihistamine:

- **ZzzQuil, Benadryl, and most store-brand sleep aids:** diphenhydramine
- **Unisom SleepTabs:** doxylamine (note that some Unisom products use diphenhydramine instead)
- **Tylenol PM:** diphenhydramine plus acetaminophen
- **Advil PM:** diphenhydramine plus ibuprofen

Using any of these to fall asleep after a night of drinking is one of the riskiest ways people combine antihistamines and alcohol. You're adding a sedative to a sedative at the exact moment you're about to lose consciousness, and the "PM" versions add a painkiller with its own alcohol warning. If alcohol is wrecking your sleep, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) has safer fixes, and our [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) guide covers the most common alternative.

### Cold and flu medicine

Night-time cold medicines usually contain a sedating antihistamine (doxylamine or chlorpheniramine), often alongside acetaminophen and a cough suppressant. The original liquid NyQuil also contains alcohol as an ingredient, though alcohol-free versions exist. Our guide to [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) covers this in detail. If a product contains acetaminophen, our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide explains why the liver risk matters.

### The "-D" decongestant versions

Claritin-D, Allegra-D, and Zyrtec-D add **pseudoephedrine**, a decongestant that works by tightening blood vessels. It can raise heart rate and blood pressure, cause jitteriness, and make it harder to sleep. Alcohol also raises heart rate and disrupts sleep, and a hangover often comes with a racing pulse. If you drink, the plain version without the "-D" is the better choice. Skip the decongestant version entirely if you have high blood pressure or heart rhythm problems unless your doctor has cleared it.

### Motion sickness pills

Dramamine (dimenhydrinate) and Bonine or "Less Drowsy" Dramamine (meclizine) are first-generation antihistamines too. People often take them on boats and flights, which are also places people drink. Treat them like Benadryl: don't combine them with alcohol.

## What About Other Allergy Medications?

People searching "allergy medication and alcohol" often aren't taking an antihistamine pill at all. Here's a quick rundown of the other common options. Check with a pharmacist about your specific product.

- **Steroid nasal sprays** such as fluticasone (Flonase) and budesonide (Rhinocort) work locally in the nose. They don't cause drowsiness and have no well-known interaction with alcohol at normal doses. For people with hay fever who drink socially, they're often a good option to discuss with a pharmacist.
- **Antihistamine nasal sprays and eye drops** such as azelastine spray or ketotifen eye drops act mostly where you apply them. Azelastine spray can cause drowsiness in some people, and its label warns against alcohol, so treat it with some caution.
- **Montelukast (Singulair)**, a prescription allergy and asthma pill, isn't a sedative and has no well-known direct interaction with alcohol. It does carry an FDA boxed warning about mood and behavior changes, so mention your drinking to the prescriber.
- **Decongestant pills** (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine) aren't antihistamines, but the heart-rate and sleep points above apply.
- **Prescription steroid pills** such as prednisone, sometimes used for severe allergic reactions, can irritate the stomach. Alcohol does too. Ask your prescriber.

## Can Alcohol Make Your Allergies Worse?

Yes, for some people, and this is worth knowing because it can send you reaching for more medicine.

- **Alcohol widens blood vessels**, including the ones in your nose. That's one reason some people get a stuffy or runny nose after drinking even without allergies.
- **Some drinks contain histamine.** Wine (especially red wine) and some beers contain histamine and other related compounds made during fermentation. Alcohol may also interfere with the enzyme your gut uses to break histamine down, though how much this matters varies from person to person.
- **Sulfites** in wine and some other drinks can trigger symptoms in sensitive people, particularly some people with asthma.
- **Population studies** have found associations between regular drinking and more hay fever and nasal symptoms, though these studies can't prove cause and effect.

If one drink reliably makes your nose run, your face flush, or your skin itch, you may be dealing with alcohol intolerance rather than ordinary allergies. Our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) walks through the signs and causes, and our [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) guide covers wine-specific triggers.

## Taking Antihistamines Before Drinking: Does It Help Flushing or Wine Headaches?

Some people take an antihistamine before drinking to prevent flushing, stuffiness, or the "wine headache." This is worth a straight answer.

**For alcohol flushing,** the classic red face after one or two drinks, common in people of East Asian descent, is usually caused by a slow version of the **ALDH2** enzyme. That enzyme is supposed to clear acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product made when your body breaks down alcohol. When it's slow, acetaldehyde builds up and causes flushing, a fast heartbeat, and nausea. Some people take an H2 blocker (like famotidine, sold as Pepcid) or an H1 antihistamine to hide the redness. These may reduce the flush, but there is no good evidence that they lower acetaldehyde. You'd be covering up the warning light while the underlying exposure continues, and long-term acetaldehyde exposure in people with this enzyme variant has been linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer. Our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers this in depth.

**For wine headaches and stuffiness,** some people do report feeling better after taking a non-drowsy antihistamine beforehand. There is no good evidence from controlled trials that this reliably prevents wine headaches, and many wine headaches likely have other causes, such as alcohol itself, dehydration, or other compounds in the wine.

**If you do try it,** use a non-drowsy option, never a first-generation drug, and keep the drinking light. If drinking causes hives, wheezing, swelling of the lips or face, or trouble breathing, that's not a "take an antihistamine and carry on" situation. See a doctor, because a true allergic reaction to something in a drink can be serious.

## Can You Use Benadryl or an Antihistamine for a Hangover?

People sometimes take Benadryl after drinking to help them sleep, or the next morning to dampen hangover symptoms. There's no good evidence that antihistamines help a hangover. Hangovers come from a mix of dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, acetaldehyde, and irritation of the stomach. Antihistamines don't address any of those, and the drowsy ones can make next-day grogginess and dry mouth worse.

The morning after, a non-drowsy antihistamine for genuine allergy symptoms is a reasonable choice for a healthy adult once the alcohol has cleared. Just don't expect it to fix the hangover.

## How Long to Wait Between Antihistamines and Alcohol

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and anyone giving you an exact number of hours is guessing. These are general patterns to help you think it through:

- **Drowsy (first-generation) antihistamines:** The sedating effects usually last several hours, and many people feel groggy the next morning, especially older adults. Hydroxyzine and doxylamine tend to last longer than diphenhydramine. A cautious approach is to skip alcohol for the rest of the day and night after a dose.
- **Once-a-day (second-generation) antihistamines:** These are designed to stay active for about 24 hours, so there isn't a realistic "gap" to wait for if you take them daily. The question is how they affect you. If you've taken your usual Allegra or Claritin for weeks without any drowsiness, a drink or two is generally lower risk than with a drowsy antihistamine. If Zyrtec or Xyzal makes you sleepy, treat it more like a drowsy one.
- **The other direction (drinking first):** If you've been drinking, avoid taking a drowsy antihistamine until the alcohol has fully cleared. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot, and after a heavy night that can stretch well into the next day.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining antihistamines and alcohol if you:

- Are **over 65**. Older adults clear these drugs more slowly and are more sensitive to confusion, falls, and urinary retention.
- Take **other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium), sleep medicines (Ambien), opioid painkillers, muscle relaxers, gabapentin or pregabalin, or sedating antidepressants. Three depressants are more dangerous than two.
- Have **sleep apnea or a lung condition**, because deep sedation can worsen breathing during sleep.
- Have **glaucoma (the narrow-angle type), an enlarged prostate, or heart rhythm problems**. First-generation antihistamines can worsen all three, and hydroxyzine has been linked to a heart-rhythm change called QT prolongation.
- Have **liver or kidney disease**, which can slow how your body clears these drugs.
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**.
- Need to **drive, operate machinery, swim, or look after children** later.

If any of these apply, a short conversation with a pharmacist is worth it. They can review your full medication list in a few minutes. For a broader look at how common medicines interact with supplements and alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink on a non-drowsy allergy pill feel nothing unusual. The serious problems come from larger doses, drowsy antihistamines, heavy drinking, or mixing in other sedatives. Antihistamine overdose, especially with diphenhydramine, can be dangerous on its own.

**Call 911 (US) or go to the emergency room if someone:**

- Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting off and can't stay awake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has blue-tinged lips or fingertips
- Has a seizure
- Is very confused, agitated, or seeing things that aren't there
- Has a very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat, or chest pain
- Is hot and flushed with dry skin and can't pee

**Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US)** if you think someone took more than the labeled dose of an antihistamine, even if they seem fine right now.

Don't leave someone who is heavily sedated to "sleep it off" alone. Roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them until help arrives.

## A Smarter Approach If You Have Allergies and Drink Socially

If you have seasonal allergies and you like the occasional drink, a few habits keep things simple:

1. **Pick a non-drowsy antihistamine** (fexofenadine or loratadine) or a steroid nasal spray for daily allergy control, and know how it affects you on a sober day.
2. **Keep drowsy antihistamines and alcohol on separate days.** That includes sleep aids, "PM" products, and night-time cold medicine.
3. **Read every label** for diphenhydramine, doxylamine, chlorpheniramine, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, pseudoephedrine, and alcohol.
4. **Drink less and slower** during allergy season, since alcohol can worsen nasal symptoms on its own. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
5. **Don't drive** after combining any antihistamine with alcohol until you're sure you're unaffected.

Some people also add supplements to their drinking routine. Here's an honest view of one we cover often. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts on GABA receptors in the brain. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising but not proven. It does **not** reverse the sedation from an antihistamine-and-alcohol combination, and there's no evidence it makes mixing them safer. If you want to try it for ordinary social drinking, popular picks include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **Drowsy antihistamines and alcohol don't mix.** Benadryl, doxylamine (Unisom, NyQuil), hydroxyzine, promethazine, chlorpheniramine, and motion sickness pills all stack with alcohol's sedation and impairment.
- **Non-drowsy antihistamines are lower risk.** Allegra and Claritin cause the least sedation. Zyrtec and Xyzal sit in between and carry an alcohol warning on the label.
- **Hidden ingredients cause much of the trouble.** "PM" products, night-time cold medicine, and "-D" decongestant versions add drugs with their own alcohol problems.
- **Antihistamines won't fix a hangover**, and using them to hide alcohol flushing covers up a warning sign rather than solving it.
- **If someone can't be woken, is breathing poorly, or has a seizure, call 911.** For a possible overdose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking antihistamines?**

It depends on which one. Older, drowsy antihistamines such as Benadryl (diphenhydramine), doxylamine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine, and promethazine should not be combined with alcohol, because both slow down the brain and the drowsiness stacks. Newer non-drowsy ones such as Allegra (fexofenadine) and Claritin (loratadine) cause much less sedation, so a drink or two is generally lower risk for a healthy adult, though you should still check the label and see how the medicine affects you first. Zyrtec (cetirizine) and Xyzal (levocetirizine) sit in between and carry an alcohol warning on the US label. Ask your pharmacist if you take other medicines.

**Which allergy medicine is safest with alcohol?**

Of the common over-the-counter options, fexofenadine (Allegra) is the least sedating, followed by loratadine (Claritin). Steroid nasal sprays such as fluticasone (Flonase) and budesonide (Rhinocort) work locally in the nose and have no well-known interaction with alcohol. None of this makes heavy drinking safe, and "safest" still means sticking to a drink or two and not driving until you know how you react.

**How long after taking Benadryl can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting period. Diphenhydramine's drowsy effects typically last several hours, and many people feel groggy into the next morning, especially older adults. A cautious approach is to skip alcohol for the rest of the day and night after a dose. If you know you'll be drinking, a non-drowsy antihistamine is a better choice for allergy symptoms, and you should talk to a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Is it dangerous to take allergy medicine after drinking?**

Taking a drowsy antihistamine like Benadryl, Unisom, or a "PM" product after a night of drinking is risky because it deepens the sedation alcohol already causes and can affect breathing and judgment while you sleep. A non-drowsy antihistamine such as Allegra or Claritin the next morning, once the alcohol has cleared, is much lower risk for a healthy adult. Read the label for hidden ingredients like acetaminophen or decongestants.

**Do antihistamines help with alcohol flushing or a red wine headache?**

Some people take antihistamines before drinking to blunt flushing or wine-related stuffiness and headaches. There is no good evidence that this works reliably for headaches, and for alcohol flushing caused by a slow ALDH2 enzyme, antihistamines may hide the redness without lowering the build-up of acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product behind it. Covering up that warning sign doesn't make drinking safer. Talk to a doctor if alcohol regularly makes you flush, wheeze, or break out in hives.

**Can you take Zyrtec or Claritin with a hangover?**

For a healthy adult, one label dose of a non-drowsy antihistamine the morning after drinking is unlikely to cause problems once the alcohol is out of your system, but it won't treat the hangover itself. It only helps allergy symptoms like a runny nose or itchy eyes. Zyrtec can make some people drowsy, which can add to hangover fatigue. Avoid the "-D" versions if you're dehydrated or your heart is racing.

**What are the signs of a dangerous reaction to antihistamines and alcohol?**

Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is very confused or hallucinating, has a seizure, has a very fast or irregular heartbeat, or has lips or fingertips turning blue. If you think someone took too much of an antihistamine, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US). Don't leave a heavily sedated person to sleep it off alone; roll them onto their side and stay with them until help arrives.
